claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten regulation of subdivided units, but the instrument should be tenancy security and habitability, not the initial rent level.
A hard cap on initial rents is the intervention that the evidence most clearly warns against.
The binding constraint named by tenants is queue length and insecurity, not price.
SDU tenants pay a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium over mainstream flats.
The median SDU tenant is a new arrival, single parent, or public-housing waiter facing a five-and-a-half-year queue.
Real rent burden has worsened from 31 to 34 percent of income.
Long-run elasticity of SDU-type supply is estimated at 0.31–0.48, so a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes roughly 3–5 percent of stock over five years.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents transfers about HK$900 per month to incumbents while leaving 3,000–4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment.
Berlin illustrates that initial-offer rents fell but listing supply contracted, and when the Mietendeckel fell, suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped increases within tenancies but not initial rents, and excluded co-living SDUs.
The SDU stock grew from 100,800 to 111,200 units across 2019–2025.
The working paper states that the stable stock reflects a second-generation, non-binding instrument, while first-generation controls on levels show consistent contraction effects.
Inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register costing 40–60 staff-years.
The subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last.
A hard cap invites judicial review and compensation claims if framed as deprivation of income, and the litigation timeline would outlast a Council term.
Mr Chan says the worst part is insecurity—two weeks' notice after asking for a window repair—and he would accept any rent to leave if the queue were three years.
The NGO survey finds 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer.

The legal opinion's middle instrument—a published, indexed per-square-foot band defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation—is compatible with this approach if paired with the missing register and inspection capacity.
The strongest objection is that a light band leaves the initial rent—the actual pain point—unregulated.
Tightening rent control on SDUs in the form of a hard initial-rent cap would help some incumbents and hurt more outsiders.
